question.text: Sequence-of-returns risk is particularly important for:

answer.text: Young investors in the accumulation phase
Retirees withdrawing from their portfolio where early losses have a disproportionately negative impact
Index fund investors with no withdrawals

explanation.text: The Logic: Sequence-of-returns risk is the risk that the order in which returns occur affects the final outcome when an investor is making ongoing withdrawals. A retiree who experiences negative returns early in the decumulation phase depletes their corpus faster, leaving less capital to recover when markets eventually rise. Two retirees with the same arithmetic average return can end up with very different outcomes purely because of the sequence of those returns. The Trap: Young accumulators are not exposed to sequence risk in the same way — they are buying into the market, so early downturns actually let them accumulate units at lower prices. Intraday traders close positions same-day and care about market timing, not multi-year sequences. Index-fund investors with no withdrawals just compound through the cycle; sequence is irrelevant when nothing is being drawn down. Note: The cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook pages reviewed in the audit cover general investment risks (interest-rate, credit, reinvestment, systematic/unsystematic) and retired-investor risk tolerance, but do not contain the specific "sequence-of-returns" term on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general industry/regulatory knowledge of retirement-withdrawal risk.
